quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Structure and Data Basics
quizzes.intro: Check whether you understand workbook architecture, rectangular data, and data types before formulas get complex.

questions.prompt: Which workbook layout best reduces long-term errors?

options.text: Put raw data, calculations, and charts mixed on one dense sheet
Separate raw data, assumptions, analysis, and presentation onto clearly named sheets
Hide everything important on a sheet named Sheet1
Store assumptions only inside chart titles

questions.explanation: Separating layers makes refresh, audit, and collaboration much safer than mixing everything together.

wrongExplanations.a: Mixed sheets are hard to sort, refresh, and audit safely.
wrongExplanations.c: Vague sheet names and hidden logic increase risk.
wrongExplanations.d: Assumptions belong in labeled input cells or an Assumptions sheet.

questions.prompt: What does rectangular data mean in Excel?

options.text: Merged title cells above every table
One header row, one field per column, and one record per row with no blank rows inside the block
Two unrelated tables placed side by side
A chart placed inside the source range

questions.explanation: Rectangular data is the foundation for reliable sorting, filtering, Tables, and PivotTables.

wrongExplanations.a: Merged headers often break sorting and references.
wrongExplanations.c: Side-by-side tables create selection and analysis hazards.
wrongExplanations.d: Charts belong on presentation sheets, not inside raw ranges.

questions.prompt: Why convert a range into an Excel Table?

options.text: Because Tables prevent all business mistakes automatically
Because Tables expand with new rows, keep formulas consistent, and support readable structured references
Because Tables delete the need for headers
Because Tables make absolute references illegal

questions.explanation: Tables improve maintenance and readability, especially as data grows.

wrongExplanations.a: Tables help structure work but do not replace judgment.
wrongExplanations.d: Absolute references are still used for assumptions and parameters.

questions.prompt: A date column sorts like text instead of chronological order. What is the most likely issue?

options.text: The chart type is wrong
The dates are stored as text rather than real Excel dates
PivotTables cannot use dates
Absolute references disable sorting

questions.explanation: Text dates often sort alphabetically. Convert them to real date values for correct chronology.

wrongExplanations.a: Chart type does not control source sorting behavior.
wrongExplanations.c: PivotTables can summarize dates when values are valid.
wrongExplanations.d: Absolute references affect formula copying, not date sorting.

questions.prompt: Which statement about values versus formatting is true?

options.text: Formatting changes the underlying calculated value automatically
Excel calculates with values; formatting only changes how values appear
Currency symbols typed into cells always remain true numbers
Left-aligned numbers are always safer than right-aligned numbers

questions.explanation: Display format and stored value are different. Confusing them causes calculation errors.

wrongExplanations.a: Formatting usually changes appearance, not the stored value.
wrongExplanations.c: Typed symbols can turn entries into text.
wrongExplanations.d: Left alignment often signals text stored where numbers were expected.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Formulas, References, and Cleaning
quizzes.intro: Apply core formula habits: references, cleaning helpers, and lookups.

questions.prompt: Cell K2 holds a tax rate. Why is =H2*$K$2 better than =H2*K2 when copying down a column?

options.text: Because relative references never work
Because $K$2 stays locked on the tax rate while H2 moves row by row
Because absolute references disable recalculation
Because K2 must be text

questions.explanation: Absolute locking keeps every copied formula pointed at the same assumption cell.

wrongExplanations.a: Relative references are useful for row inputs like H2.
wrongExplanations.d: The tax rate should be numeric, not text.

questions.prompt: Which formula best standardizes a messy customer name for analysis while preserving the raw column?

options.text: Overwrite the raw name cells manually with no history
=PROPER(TRIM([@[Customer Name]]))
=SUM([@[Customer Name]])
=XLOOKUP([@[Customer Name]],A:A,A:A)

questions.explanation: Helper formulas like TRIM and PROPER clean visibly without destroying source values.

wrongExplanations.c: SUM is for numbers, not names.
wrongExplanations.d: A self-lookup does not clean spaces or casing.

questions.prompt: What is the safest beginner default for XLOOKUP matching keys?

options.text: Approximate match for every product code
Exact match, with a clear not-found result
Ignore missing keys entirely
Always return the first column only

questions.explanation: Exact match with explicit not-found handling prevents silent wrong joins.

wrongExplanations.a: Approximate match is for ordered ranges, not ordinary codes.
wrongExplanations.c: Missing keys should be visible for data quality review.
wrongExplanations.d: XLOOKUP can return any chosen return column.

questions.prompt: Why keep thresholds such as high-discount cutoffs on an Assumptions sheet?

options.text: So nobody can ever change them
So one labeled input can update many formulas safely and transparently
Because Excel forbids numbers inside formulas
Because PivotTables cannot read formulas

questions.explanation: Central assumptions make models easier to update, review, and trust.

wrongExplanations.a: Assumptions should be editable by design, with control and documentation.
wrongExplanations.c: Excel allows hardcoded numbers, but they are harder to audit.
wrongExplanations.d: PivotTables can summarize calculated fields from source Tables.

questions.prompt: A check formula returns SUM(Net)+SUM(Discount)-SUM(Gross) = 0. What does that mainly prove?

options.text: The business strategy is optimal
The workbook's revenue arithmetic is internally consistent
Every lookup matched perfectly
No filters are active

questions.explanation: Reconciliation checks validate internal arithmetic before presentation.

wrongExplanations.a: Consistency is not the same as strategic success.
wrongExplanations.d: Filter state must be checked independently.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Analysis, Dashboards, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Use the full lesson. Focus on PivotTables, presentation, and professional judgment.

questions.prompt: In a PivotTable of net revenue by region, Excel shows Count instead of Sum. What should you do first?

options.text: Accept Count because it looks similar
Open Value Field Settings and set the aggregation to Sum after checking the source data types
Delete the PivotTable permanently
Convert revenue to text

questions.explanation: Wrong aggregations are common when source values are text or blank-heavy. Fix the summary settings and data types.

wrongExplanations.a: Count and Sum answer different questions.
wrongExplanations.c: Deletion is unnecessary if settings can be corrected.
wrongExplanations.d: Text conversion would worsen numeric aggregation.

questions.prompt: Which chart choice best compares monthly revenue trends across regions?

options.text: A 3D pie chart
A line chart with one line per region over months
A single KPI card with no time axis
Conditional formatting only

questions.explanation: Line charts make multi-series trends over time easy to compare.

wrongExplanations.a: Pie charts are poor for trends and 3D distorts perception.
wrongExplanations.c: A KPI card cannot show comparative monthly movement.
wrongExplanations.d: Formatting can highlight values but is not a trend comparison chart.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a beginner dashboard notes panel?

options.text: Secret macros with no explanation
Data source, refresh date, key definitions, and known limitations
Only decorative clip art
Raw unfiltered transaction rows

questions.explanation: Notes create trust by documenting provenance and caveats.

wrongExplanations.c: Decoration does not explain the numbers.
wrongExplanations.d: Raw rows belong on data sheets, not the dashboard canvas.

questions.prompt: Before a leadership meeting, which action is most important?

options.text: Add more colors until the sheet looks busy
Refresh PivotTables, confirm filters, reconcile key totals, and scan for errors
Hardcode over any formula that looks inconvenient
Delete the Assumptions sheet to save space

questions.explanation: A short audit checklist prevents presenting stale, filtered, or inconsistent numbers.

wrongExplanations.a: Visual noise does not equal readiness.
wrongExplanations.c: Hardcoding hides logic and creates future errors.
wrongExplanations.d: Assumptions documentation is part of trust.

questions.prompt: Why are ratios like discount rate risky to sum directly across rows?

options.text: Because Excel cannot store percentages
Because ratios are often non-additive; numerators and denominators should be aggregated first
Because PivotTables forbid averages
Because all ratios are already totals

questions.explanation: Additive measures can be summed; many ratios cannot. Aggregate components, then compute the ratio.

wrongExplanations.a: Excel stores percentages as numeric values.
wrongExplanations.c: PivotTables can average, but average of ratios may still be misleading.
wrongExplanations.d: A rate is not automatically a total.

questions.prompt: Which statement shows mature Excel judgment?

options.text: If a chart looks polished, the analysis must be correct
Structure, definitions, reconciliation, and clear presentation matter more than decorative complexity
Hardcoding replaces the need for assumptions
Raw data should be edited in place until it matches the desired story

questions.explanation: Reliable Excel work is a discipline of structure and verification, not visual flair.

wrongExplanations.a: Polish can hide wrong ranges or aggregations.
wrongExplanations.c: Hardcoding makes updates and audits harder.
wrongExplanations.d: Editing raw data to fit a narrative destroys trust.
